title: IT Support Specialist Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)
meta_description: A complete IT support specialist resume example: help desk, ticketing, troubleshooting, and the exact bullet formula that turns resolved tickets into proof hiring managers and applicant tracking systems both reward.
content_html:
IT Support Specialist Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

An IT support specialist resume has one job: prove you can keep people working, not just close tickets. Hiring managers do not hire for tool lists or pleasant adjectives. They hire for problems solved, users back on their feet, and systems that stay fixed: the ticket you resolved, the user you helped, and the result that followed.

Quick answer: An IT support specialist resume should include a summary naming your strongest support outcome, a skills section with the ticketing systems, operating systems, and remote-support tools you actually use, experience bullets pairing each fix with the result it produced, and certifications such as CompTIA A+. Resolved tickets prove the craft; the resume proves the judgment behind them.

Key Takeaways

  • Every experience bullet follows the same formula: problem + action + outcome — the ticket you took, the fix you made, the result it produced.
  • Lead with your support outcome and your numbers: tickets resolved each week, most fixed on first contact, response times kept inside the service target.
  • Spell tools exactly as postings do — ServiceNow, Jira, Windows, macOS, Active Directory — they are literal ATS keyword filters.
  • Show impact through counts and honest ranges, never through vague duties: name the result.
  • Keep the file itself single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask a hiring manager what separates a keep-forever IT support specialist from a risky one:

  • Tickets that actually close. Problems solved at the root, not patched and reopened next week.
  • Users who feel helped. Plain-language explanations, patience under pressure, and follow-ups that close the loop.
  • Speed without sloppiness. Fast first responses and fixes that hold, with the service target met week after week.
  • Documentation that saves the next person. Knowledge-base articles, runbooks, and clear ticket notes other specialists can follow.
  • Judgment about escalation. Knowing when to solve it yourself, when to hand it up, and when to flag a wider outage.

IT Support Specialist Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is an example for an IT support specialist at a mid-size company. It’s fictional — names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: problem, action, outcome.

CHIOMAKA EZE
Abuja · (234) 555-0162 · chiomaka.eze@email.com · linkedin.com/in/chiomakaeze

SUMMARY
IT support specialist with 4 years keeping a 200-person company working, currently owning the help desk queue for a logistics firm with offices in 3 cities. Resolve 60 tickets a week with 82% fixed on first contact, hold a 96% service-target record, and wrote the team’s first knowledge base. Known for calm explanations, fast fixes, and problems that stay fixed.

SKILLS
ServiceNow · Jira Service Management · Windows 10/11 · macOS · Active Directory · Microsoft 365 · Google Workspace · Remote desktop · VPN · Printer and network troubleshooting · Hardware imaging · Knowledge-base writing · Slack · Zoom

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

IT Support Specialist — SwiftHaul Logistics, Abuja | 2022–Present

  • Own the help desk queue for 200 staff across 3 offices: 60 tickets a week, 82% fixed on first contact, and a 96% record of meeting the 4-hour service target.
  • Cut password-reset tickets by a third after writing a self-service guide and walking new starters through it on day one, freeing the queue for harder problems.
  • Built the team’s first knowledge base: 40 articles covering the 20 most common fixes, now used by the whole support team and linked in ticket replies.
  • Set up 120 new starters in 2 years — accounts, laptops, email, and access — with zero missed first-day logins after introducing a pre-boarding checklist.
  • Spotted a failing office printer fleet from repeat tickets and pushed a vendor fix, cutting printer tickets from 15 a week to 2.

Junior IT Support Technician — Capital Business School, Abuja | 2021–2022

  • Supported 90 staff and 400 students: classroom projectors, staff laptops, and the student Wi-Fi network, with most issues fixed the same day.
  • Imaged and deployed 60 laptops for a new computer lab in 2 weeks, working from a checklist that caught 3 faulty drives before handover.
  • Ran the weekly backup check and flagged 2 failed backups before data was lost, earning the school’s first documented recovery test.
  • Answered the support line with a calm, plain-language script that cut repeat calls about the same issue by a quarter.

EDUCATION
HND Computer Science — Federal Polytechnic, Nasarawa | 2019–2021

CERTIFICATIONS
CompTIA A+ (2022) · CompTIA Network+ in progress · Microsoft 365 Fundamentals (2023)

How to Write Each Section

The summary: one outcome, one proof

Your summary is two or three sentences: your role, your years, your strongest support outcome, and the proof. “IT support specialist with 4 years keeping a 200-person company working, 60 tickets a week with most fixed on first contact” tells a hiring manager everything in one breath. Skip the generic opener about passion — the outcome is the opener.

The skills section: tools you can defend

List the ticketing systems, operating systems, and remote-support tools you genuinely use, spelled exactly as postings spell them: ServiceNow, Jira, Windows, macOS, Active Directory, Microsoft 365. These are literal keyword filters for applicant tracking systems. Leave off tools you only watched someone else use — an interviewer will ask.

Experience bullets: ticket, fix, result

Every bullet starts with the problem, then the fix, then the result: “cut password-reset tickets by a third after writing a self-service guide”; “set up 120 new starters with zero missed first-day logins.” Duties without results read as filler. Where exact figures were never tracked, use honest ranges — “most fixed on first contact” beats a guessed number.

Certifications and education: near the top, never buried

Certifications belong close to the top for support roles: CompTIA A+ is the one hiring managers look for first, and listing it early gets your resume past the first screen. If you are studying for a certification, say so plainly — “CompTIA Network+ in progress” beats silence. Education follows the same rule: name the qualification, the school, and the year.

IT Support Specialist Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s exact language and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Ticketing & help desk: ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Zendesk, Freshdesk, ticket triage, SLA management, escalation (only the depth you genuinely have).
  • Systems & networks: Windows 10/11, macOS, Active Directory, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, VPN, DNS, DHCP, Wi-Fi troubleshooting.
  • Hardware & devices: Laptop imaging, printer troubleshooting, hardware diagnostics, asset management, mobile device setup.
  • People & process: Remote support, user training, knowledge-base writing, documentation, customer service, incident communication.

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. IT support resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting. Start from a clean template gallery or resume builder option, then verify with the free ATS grader.

5 Mistakes That Cost IT Support Specialist Interviews

  1. Duties without results. “Responsible for help desk tickets” says nothing about what changed. Every bullet needs a problem, a fix, and a result.
  2. Jargon aimed at users. Name the ticket, the fix, and the result in plain words.
  3. Tools without matching bullets. A tool list proves nothing on its own. Pair each tool with work that used it: the queue you cleared, the remote session you ran, the device you imaged.
  4. Hiding the people skills. If every bullet is a system and none is a user helped, the resume reads like a server manual.
  5. Unreadable formatting. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, and image-based PDFs scramble parsing, so your certifications arrive as word soup. One column, standard headings, real text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in an IT support specialist resume?

A summary naming your strongest support outcome; a skills section with the ticketing systems, operating systems, and remote-support tools you actually use; experience bullets pairing each fix with the result it produced; and certifications such as CompTIA A+. Resolved tickets prove the craft; the resume proves the judgment behind them.

How is an IT support specialist resume different from a systems administrator resume?

An IT support specialist resume proves you can keep people working: tickets resolved, users helped, devices set up, and problems explained in plain language. A systems administrator resume proves you can keep the infrastructure itself running: servers, networks, backups, and security. Support is user-facing and ticket-driven; administration is system-facing and project-driven. Many roles blend both, so lead with the side the posting asks for.

Do I need a CompTIA A+ certification to get an IT support job?

Not always, but it helps a lot for a first help desk role: it is the certification hiring managers and applicant tracking systems look for first, and it signals you know hardware, operating systems, networking, and troubleshooting. Hands-on experience can substitute for it — a home lab, volunteer support work, or a previous customer-facing role. List it near the top of your resume; if you are studying for it, say so plainly.

How do I show impact on an IT support resume when most of my work is tickets?

Turn tickets into outcomes: tickets resolved each week, first-contact resolution, response times kept inside the service target, repeat issues fixed at the root, and knowledge-base articles that let users help themselves. “Resolved 60 tickets a week with most fixed on first contact” proves far more than “responsible for help desk tickets.” Count what you can, and use honest ranges where exact figures were never tracked.

What if I have no help desk experience yet?

Lead with the closest equivalent work: the computer you fixed for a neighbour, the small office you kept running, the volunteer role where you set up accounts, or the retail job where you solved problems for frustrated people. Then frame each as support work in miniature, add a home lab and a CompTIA A+ in progress, run your resume through a free ATS grader first, and target entry-level help desk roles as stepping stones.

Should an IT support specialist resume list every tool I have touched?

No — list the tools you can defend in an interview, spelled exactly as postings spell them. A long list of ticketing systems and remote tools with no matching bullets reads thin, so pair each one with work that used it: the queue you cleared, the remote session you ran, the device you imaged. Three tools with proof beat ten without any.
